title: Living in Vow 1
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of clarity, compassion, and accountability in Buddhist communities, particularly when it comes to addressing issues of abuse and harm. Zoketsu Norman Fischer encourages the community to examine their own practices and teachings, acknowledging both the positive and negative aspects of Buddhism, and to work towards reformulation and reform. Ultimately, the talk highlights the value of dedication, devotion, and humility in spiritual practice, particularly through the practice of Zazen (meditation), which is rooted in the Bodhisattva's vow to help all beings.

sentences.text: It's really nice to be here.
My body remembers so many years of being here at a certain rhythm, so now that I'm here, I think, oh, it's been too long, I missed a visit or something.
I'm always glad to be here, but especially now.
Tim sent me links to Thales's Shuso Talks.
It's great, this stuff: you can send links and listen.
I can listen to Thales talking, and I think he's the first Shuso in my memory to tell his life story backwards.
It's a really good idea.
Leave it to Thales to think of something like that.
From what I listened to, his Way Seeking Mind Talk and one of his classes, it sounds like the practice period is going beautifully.
So for those of you here in Bellingham who are in the fall practice period, congratulations.
It's especially nice for me to know that the practice period goes on in such a good way in my absence.

Because I was able to listen to the links, I'm at least a little bit caught up on what you've all been talking about, and I appreciated Tim speaking last night because that filled me in a little more on the themes you've been working with.
But I'm not entirely caught up, so I apologize in advance if what I talk about this weekend doesn't relate to what you've been considering.
The way these things go, it always turns out that everything relates to everything, so probably it's okay.

What I want to talk about this weekend is a wonderful book we've been reading and discussing in our Dharma seminar at home, by Shohaku Okumura, who's one of our real Dharma treasures, a Soto Zen priest from Japan who has lived many years in America.
He's a wonderful teacher and scholar, and he's written a book recently from his talks called *Living by Vow*.
We've been studying it at home, so I'd like to talk about some of the things I've been learning from him.
Before I do that, I actually want to talk about something else that's unrelated.
It's very unpleasant, and I don't want to talk about it, but I feel that I should, despite my reluctance.
All I'm going to do is read you a post that's up on the Sweeping Zen website, [unclear: "misunderstanding the title"].
Maybe some of you have seen it on Sweeping Zen.
This is what the post says.

*I have been frankly disgusted over the recent stories about Zen teachers' sexual misconduct, and that is a mild term for some of the abuse that has been reported, these reports that have appeared in the national press, in the New York Times, and in Zen online circles and elsewhere.

What's been so awful is not only the conduct itself, though this conduct itself is certainly really bad, dismaying, terrible, discouraging, but what's been worse for me is this wearying sense of deja vu.
How often can this keep happening?
How long will we have to endure it before it's over?
How long are we going to continue to be so destructively clueless?

Honestly, I've been so disgusted by this that I've been more or less ignoring it, ignoring the stories, not wanting to think about it, not wanting to write about it, not wanting to talk about it, not particularly proud of myself for this attitude.
But really, after all this time, I can't hardly take it anymore.
It is so repetitive.
It is so tiresome.
And you would ignore it altogether if it weren't for how terribly wounding it is to so many people.
I'm really, really thankful for my several Zen colleagues who have been active and proactive in writing about this and speaking out and doing things to oppose these excesses.
And I'm grateful to Sweeping Zen, this website that is now a venue for people to be able to speak out.*
*I feel as if all these people are working on my behalf and with my support in speaking out actively, as I hope I would be doing if they were not.
How can the Gempos, Eidos, and Sasakis of the world do this stuff when they know that of course they're going to be outed?
Of course they are.
How can they do it when they know that?
How can they think that their guys just need to have some fun spirit?
It is not fun for the people who are on the other end of their excesses.
People's lives are really ruined by this.
They're really hurting people.
How can they do it?
It's really quite unbelievable to me.
I can't understand it.
How is it possible?
I thought about this and I thought, well, there are three possibilities.*
*First, they have no impulse control, like addicts.
They can't stop.
This is sad and pitiful in the case of most addicts, and we're sympathetic and we understand that.
We would be sympathetic to them too if it weren't for the fact that they don't say they're addicts.
They claim instead that they're spiritual masters doing this, and that makes it different.
So they have no impulse control, maybe.
Or secondly, maybe they think that they're enlightened, and that being enlightened they are immune from moral constraints.
Maybe they think that their sexual partners should celebrate the fact that they get to crawl into bed with an enlightened person, and all the goodness that will flow from that wonderful experience.
Maybe that's what they think.
Or maybe it's not those things.
Maybe they just don't notice or care whether or not they're hurting someone.
Maybe they just don't think about it.
Well, no matter what explains it, and maybe we can't explain it, I find it hard to affirm such people as Buddhist teachers.
I've read sutras and I've seen a lot of Buddhist teachers and I've thought about this for a long time.*
*It would seem to me that one would expect an actual Buddhist teacher to have a certain amount of impulse control, right?
You would think that spiritual teachers would not be slaves to their desires.

You would think that it would be a characteristic of theirs that they would care about the well-being of others, and furthermore that they would have some capacity at least to understand what kinds of conduct would hurt others, and that they would forbear from doing that.
As to the enlightenment argument, to me this is worst of all.
I can't imagine how anybody could think that the word enlightenment refers to a permanent state of transcendence that someone possesses somehow as a sort of character trait.
My studies over the years tell me that in Buddhism the idea of spiritual enlightenment precisely contains the notion that one cannot possess anything exclusive of others.*
*So modesty and radical caring would be enlightenment's characterological marks, not swagger and entitlement.
Now, to be sure, it must be the case that these people have tremendous spiritual powers.
Obviously they do.
Otherwise, how could they have inspired so many people for so long?
But being a Buddhist teacher, it seems to me, is not just a matter of possessing spiritual powers per se.
Lots of people possess spiritual powers and they can perform spiritual feats.
That's very interesting, and if you like that kind of thing, good.
But that's not the same as being a Buddhist teacher.
Maybe because of these powers they can inspire other people and encourage them.
And good, that's good.
So we shouldn't complain about anybody who has been inspired by them and maybe has had long years of practice and will continue their practice.
Good.
And I'm sure that the gratitude that such people feel really is heartfelt.
I'm happy for these offenders if they can also have the satisfaction of having done some good, along with what I hope is the anguish and the shame that they feel, too, for having done so much bad.*
*But let's not be confused by this.
Crimes are crimes and people who commit them are to be condemned.
Compassion and genuine gratitude don't change this fact.
In fact, they reinforce it.
Clarity about right and wrong is a great and compassionate gift that we can give to someone who is in need of such a gift.
It's one of the greatest, most compassionate gifts that we can give.*
You can see how exasperated I get.
*So then there's all that.
Okay, there's all that.
But of course it's more complicated than that.
Of course it would be nice if we could all say, well, there's just a bunch of evil Zen masters out there who perpetrate crimes all by themselves, and the rest of us have nothing to do with it.
No.
In every case, this only can happen with the full collusion of a community.
It couldn't be possible.
One person can't do that much harm unless there's lots of cooperation and collusion.

And of course, as we all know, when we get into the complexities of these individual stories, because every case is different and every little wrinkle is different, sometimes the victims are willing or partly willing or maybe willing or could be willing, we don't know.
But this doesn't matter.
It doesn't excuse the conduct, because the teachers are the ones who have to know better and be responsible.
They're the responsible parties.*
*But it's even worse than that.

When you observe this over an entire lifetime of practice, you do get the feeling eventually that there must be something wrong with Zen or Buddhism or religion, because it would be nice if we could say only Zen people do this.
Only Buddhists do this.

But just check your local Catholic parish and you'll see that it's not only Zen or Buddhists that do it, and of course it's not only religious people that do it, but there's a particularly toxic quality to it when it happens in the religious world.
So it would be very easy and nice to just blame the perps and leave it at that.
Well, there's a few really bad people and we can get rid of them and we'll be fine.
It would be nice if we could just blame those communities and those cultures.
Well, those guys, no wonder, they had a bunch of bad 60s ideas, gurus, and they came of age in the 70s, naturally they do this stuff.
And we'll all be beyond this soon, it'll never happen again.
No, it's worse than that, it's more subtle than that.

We have to ask ourselves, what is it about Buddhist teachings, Buddhist rituals, Buddhist practice, with the position of the teacher at the center of it all, that seems to encourage these mistakes and make them worse?*

*Did we all really think that we could simply take on an Asian religion nurtured in the soils of an alien, feudalistic society and just swallow it whole without also swallowing a bunch of probably toxic and basic misunderstandings that would inevitably require some crucial rethinking and reformulation?
Did we really think that we were going to do that?
This leaves us all with a lot of responsibility and a lot of work, with lots of thoughtful discussion ahead, lots of reformatting and reformulation of what we do as we are doing.
There's lots of soul searching we all have to do.
This is going to take a long time, it's going to take sensitivity, it's going to take intelligence, and it's going to take, one of the themes of this practice period, courage to figure this out.
But we will figure it out.*
*Buddhism and religion in general has too much goodness in it and too much positive power in it, a goodness and a positive power that we absolutely need in these troubled times we're living in.
So we can't just say, as many have said, understandably, to hell with religion.
Forget it, who could blame them?
But we need these practices and these teachings.
There's too much good in them to abandon them.
That goodness will bear the scrutiny, and it will lead to good results eventually.
So we can't give up the struggle here.
All we have to do is take a deep breath, cease as much as we can from the general confusion that such events foster.
This is the trouble: there's such general confusion in the wake of it, and bad feelings and mutual recrimination and so on and so on.
We can stop that more confusion and just do what it takes to address the damages and get back to work, because we have a lot to do.
And I pray and I hope and I really believe that our practice communities are not so subject to this kind of abuse as those communities were, for many, many reasons.*
*We have lots of empowered elders and teachers and they talk to each other and give each other feedback.
So students know there's not just one person that they can talk to.
There are many people that they can talk to.
Also, I hope and I pray and I believe that we have fostered an atmosphere in which there is no conspiracy of silence.
There is no pressure not to speak out when you feel something is wrong.
We can and we do speak openly, even though sometimes it's difficult to do so.
Again, courage.*
*I believe that.
I'm not worried really about our communities.
Still, we cannot congratulate ourselves, and it would be a mistake to imagine that other and more subtle, if less toxic, forms of abuse aren't possible even in our own communities.
We have to have a little bit of humility about that.
But trust is really important in spiritual practice, and it's really necessary that we trust one another.
We can't go around practicing this intimate practice feeling defensive or suspicious of one another.
And I really do think that we can be confident of each other's sincerity.
That means everybody, from the person who comes in the door the first time to the most senior of our teachers.
Everybody is sincerely trying.
Everybody wants not to do harm.
Still, I bring all this up although it's unpleasant and it's not what I want to talk about, because it's good to bring these things up from time to time to kind of remind us to pause, to think.
It's time to take a breath before we continue with our practice.*
So now I'll continue to talk about something else.
In the very beginning of his book he says, ordinary people are those who live being pulled by their karma.
Bodhisattvas are those who live by their vows.

His book is actually very useful, and I recommend it to all those who practice regularly, because in it he talks about almost all the little verses that we chant: the verse that we'll chant in the moment before vows, the repentance verse, the verse we chant in the morning before putting on the okesa.
These things we do all the time, the meal chant and all that.
He discusses them in the book, so it's quite wonderful for those of us who are familiar with these short texts.
So, ordinary people live pulled by their karma.
Bodhisattvas live by their vows.
What is karma?
It's our inheritance.
Our conditioning.
Our desires.
Our needs.
Maybe our values.
Certainly our actions, our habits, the results of our actions, our habits.
This is our life: karma.
Vows, what's that?
Well, this is what we spend our lives trying to understand.
What does it mean to live by vow?
What does it mean to shift from living by karma to living by vow?
How would we know if we were making that shift?
What would it feel like?
These are the questions of our lifetime.
Shohaku says it's not that you abandon your karma and leap into your vow.
No, when you live by vow, karma is still there.
Of course it is.
But the question is, and each one of us for ourselves has to be really honest in answering it, where is the commitment?
Is it to our karma, to our needs, our desires, our values, our hopes, our fears, our habits?
Or is it to our vow?
When you live by vow, it's the commitment.
Vow is the anchor point.
It's the purpose, the inspiration, the direction, the vision for your life.
One of the wonderful and unexpected things is that in Soto Zen we follow the teachings, of course, of Dogen and of Suzuki Roshi, who made such a beautiful expression of Dogen for our time and place.
In their view, vow is the same thing as Zazen.
You wouldn't expect that.
For them, when we sit in Zazen, we're not meditating.
Zen Buddhists don't meditate.
We sit in Zazen.
Sitting in Zazen is sitting in the middle of our vow.
And the vow is not some kind of promise that we make to accomplish something, which is what we usually think of as vow, like a New Year's Eve resolution.
Vow is bigger than that.
Vow is to sit in the middle of Buddha's life.
And Shohaku here is quoting Katagiri Roshi, who was one of our teachers.
This is a wonderful expression of Zazen.
He says, "In Zazen, many things come up."
We can relate to this, right?
We've been sitting here this morning.
We know.
Yes, many things come up.
"Thoughts, emotions, sometimes even anger or hatred.
But all you have to do is take care of Zazen in eternal possibility."
Isn't that good?
What does he mean?
Who knows?
Sounds good, doesn't it?
All we have to do is take care of Zazen in eternal possibility.
It's completely beyond good or bad, right or wrong.
So put aside all kinds of imagination fabricated by your consciousness.
Don't attach to thoughts and emotions.
Just let them return to emptiness.
They can come.
Try to get rid of them.
But just let them return to emptiness.
Just be present there and swim in Buddha nature.
I remember Katagiri Roshi was constantly talking about swimming, which he had the most charming way of pronouncing in English.
I can't imitate it.
Swimming in Buddha nature.
That's what we're doing when we're sitting in zazen.
We're swimming in Buddha nature.
This is living the Bodhisattva's vow to help all beings.
Then the great energy of the universe supports you, and you take one step toward the future with all beings.
That's what we're here to do this weekend on our cushions.
Katagiri Roshi eventually went to Minnesota and established the center there, and he called his temple Living by Vow Temple, which is where the book gets its title.
When Katagiri Roshi passed away, untimely, very young, they invited Shohaku Okumura to come and teach there for a few years, and so he did.
Vowing is, of course, the key element in all Mahayana Buddhism and all Bodhisattva paths in Buddhism.
Vowing is at the center.

It's especially important for us as Soto Zen practitioners, because our practice is so much focused on devotion and dedication to ongoing practice, much more than we're focused on knowledge and accomplishment and spiritual powers, experiences.
What we're focused on is devotion to ongoing practice.
Suzuki Roshi used to joke that this is a very good practice for stupid, incompetent people, because you don't have to be able to do great things.
All you have to do is just doggedly keep on.
He used to joke.
He said, "I would have quit when I was young, but I wasn't smart enough to realize I could escape."
The older I get, the more I can relate to that.
I think to myself, "Why aren't I doing something else?
I could have done this, I could have done that."
I couldn't think of anything else to do.
So it's true, it's a good practice for stupid people.
Even though there are a lot of smart people who do it, maybe the stupid part of them is doing it.
In fact, I think that's it, don't you?
But it's not just that we're a bunch of losers and that's why we have this teaching.
I think it comes from a very profound thought in Dogen's teaching: what is knowledge and accomplishment and spiritual height?
What is it?
That's what it is.
If you really look and see what the highest spiritual knowledge is, that's what it is.
It's dedication and devotion to ongoing practice.
It's recognition that to do the practice is to swim in Buddha nature, to step into eternal possibility, into the future with everyone, one step at a time.
And nothing could be more elevated or more profound than that.
So that's why we so much affirm this value of dedication to practice, determination, softness, and ongoing practice.
If you read the book, you'll see that in the beginning Shohaku has a long section about the different styles within Soto Zen, all the different lineage families.
Every lineage family has a slightly different style.

Shohaku is saying, "I came from the Sawaki Kodo lineage family, and then I go to the Minnesota Zen Center, where Katagiri was the founder, and he came from the Hashimoto Roshi style, and then the Suzuki Roshi style."
All the lineages are a little bit different.
He talks about it, but it's not important to say how they're different; it's just interesting.
Just like in your own family, every family has a little bit different characteristic.
So in lineage families, also, there's a distinct characteristic.
I've noticed this in the Suzuki Roshi lineage, where now we have lots of groups and lots of teachers, and everybody is so different.
Like in your own family, siblings are all so different, and at the same time there's a similarity in the family style.
The Katagiri style that he inherited from his teacher was more careful attention to the details of form and ritual.
The style that Shohaku inherited from Sawaki Kodo was this very hard-ass style of very long periods of zazen, one after the other.
He used to say, "Zazen with no toys."
By toys, he meant things like dharma talks, dokusan, service, chanting.
They didn't do any of that.
They would just sit there on and on and on and on.
And poor Shohaku, who's I think exactly my age, maybe even a little younger, his body is completely falling apart now.
His knees are gone because they practiced so hard.
The Suzuki Roshi style is a little more gentle.
The Suzuki Roshi way is more like living in a country temple.
People come, you do a little services for them and stuff like that.
So there's ritual, but we don't worry too much about it.
It's a do-our-best kind of feeling.
When Suzuki Roshi wanted to establish proper monastic ritual at San Francisco Zen Center, he got other people to come, because he either didn't know it very well or didn't care that much.
He would get other people to come and teach everybody how to do it.
Anyway, wow.
His commitment to the impossible.
We chant the four vows: *Beings are numberless, I vow to save them all.* Well, that's impossible.
So vow, in our practice, is commitment to something that is beyond what can be done, certainly in one lifetime, but even in myriad lifetimes.
In other words, it's not something you plan on accomplishing.
It's a direction that you're going in.
It's a dedication, a firm pillar that holds up your life.
This is why vow, if you really understand vow, makes you humble.
And humility is a very big virtue in Soto Zen, and especially in our Dharma family.
Think about it.
If you vow to take up an infinite task, you're not going to get that far, are you?
Even if you accomplish a tremendous amount, more than any human being has ever accomplished, it would be nothing compared to infinity, right?
Nothing.
So our efforts in practice are always going to amount to almost nothing.
That makes you humble, right?
"How are you doing?"
"Well, I accomplished almost nothing."
On the other hand, you're not discouraged by this, and you certainly are not self-deprecating about it, because you have in fact made this commitment, and it is a fantastic noble commitment.
Maybe the highest commitment a human being could dedicate themselves to, so you feel good about that.
You're not completely wallowing in the mud there.
Besides, nobody's done any better with this commitment than you have, right?
It's not like somebody else is doing better.
So in other words, you're humble, but on the other hand, you're not thinking that everybody else is better off than you are.
We're all in the same boat, exactly.
But it is a beautiful thing, and a dignified thing, and something that one can really appreciate, knowing that you've committed yourself to walking in the direction.
Even though you're never getting there, you're going.
That's what you're doing, no doubt.
That's really good, and we take a lot of satisfaction and joy in that.
It's also why, contrary to what one might imagine, and this is also something Shohaku talks about, the idea of atonement and repentance is intimately connected to the idea of vow.
He says something in the book which is very, very important.
He says, *the awareness of incompleteness is repentance.* Isn't that good?
*The awareness of incompletion is repentance.* In other words, of course we're going to make mistakes.
We're not going to be so good at our practice.
We're human.
We have to take our mistakes seriously and repent for them.
That's just our practice.
He discusses the Bodhisattva's vows, our basic and most fundamental vows.

One thing I learned, which I didn't realize, is that if you do research as he has done, you find out, it's kind of interesting, that the four vows are connected to the four noble truths, and he explains how that is.
*Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.* That relates to the first noble truth, all conditioned existence is suffering.
But since the Bodhisattva vow is essentially an altruistic vow, and always involves practicing for and with others, we don't just vow to deeply understand the truth of suffering.
We vow to save all beings from suffering.
*Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.* It's the second noble truth, the cause of suffering, which is delusion, or grasping.

Grasping, not because grasping is morally bad and we shouldn't do it, but because when we grasp at something that we think we can have, but actually we can't have it, because it isn't what we think it is, we're going to suffer.
Our life is a dream.
There's nothing to grasp, and there's nobody there to grasp anything.
Until we know that, we're going to suffer a lot.
So our practice is over and over and over again letting go, letting go, letting go, of every thought letting go.
We can't grasp that thought.
It's suffering.
And here again, we don't just vow to understand and practice this, we vow to overcome it, no matter how endless this delusion is, no matter how much it is everywhere and in everyone.
We're going to end all of it, for everyone, and with everyone.
*Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.* Interestingly, this third great vow relates to the fourth noble truth.
Dharma gates are the path.
In classical Buddhism, it's the eightfold path: right view, right intention, right speech, right livelihood, etc., etc.
But in the case of the Bodhisattva vow, there are endless Dharma gates, not just eight or ten or 37 or 108, endless.
And we vow to enter all of them, to open up every gate, for and with everyone.
In the last vow, *Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to attain it.* This is the third of the four noble truths, the truth of nirvana, the end of suffering.
This is the way of the Buddha, the way of nirvana, peacefulness, coolness, end of suffering.
Unsurpassable.
It's beyond compare because it isn't anything.
So how could you compare it?
And we vow to attain it, even though it's unattainable, for and with everyone.
I was trying to think, how come the third and fourth truths are reversed in the case of the vows?
I don't really know, but in actual practice it seems like first you realize, "Oh, there's a lot of suffering here."
Then you realize, "There's got to be a way out of this.
What's the cause?"
And then you start practicing.
You don't end suffering and then practice.
You practice and then end suffering.
So that's why it kind of makes sense.
Here's the early version of the four vows that makes it clear how they're related to the four noble truths.
*I vow to enable people to be released from the truth of suffering.
I vow to enable people to understand the truth of the origin of suffering.
I vow to enable people to peacefully settle down in the truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
I vow to enable people to enter the cessation of suffering that is Nirvana.*
That's apparently an early version of the same vow.
But Shohaku, in commenting on that, says that in that version the implication is, "I, having achieved these things, now I'm going to turn around and help others to achieve them."
It sounds like the person making the vow has accomplished these things and now they're going to vow to help others accomplish them.
But in the four vows as we chant them now, when you think about it, the assumption is that we have not yet attained the way.
We still are overwhelmed by the numberless sentient beings.
We don't yet realize there are no beings to be saved.
We still are floored by the inexhaustible delusions.
We don't yet realize there are no delusions.
So this is the greatness of the four vows.
They acknowledge that even though we're miserable, ordinary, confused people, nevertheless we are vowing to overcome not only our own confusion but that of endless others.
To me this is even more fantastic, that we would take such a vow, confused as we are, that we would say, "Doesn't matter.
I don't have to pretend that I'm not who I am.
I'm going to be who I am, and I'm going to nevertheless undertake this."
This is even greater to me.
This is one of the great things, I think, about our practice: it fully acknowledges human confusion as at the center of the path.
Not to be denigrated or abandoned, but to be embraced as the Bodhisattva's way.
Since we are ordinary human beings and guaranteed to keep making mistakes, we have a lot of repentance to do.

The idea is, as long as we're not Buddhas, we're going to have to be repenting and confessing constantly, because all of our actions, even the ones that we think are good, will inevitably have the taint of selfishness.
Therefore, even though we think we have good intentions, we may be causing harm to others without knowing or doing it.
Most of the time we do repent for our selfish actions, the ones we know are selfish.
But also we have to repent for all of our actions, all of the time.
We are purified by our acts of repentance, and we are forgiven over and over and over again.
And then the next minute, more purification.

In his chapter Shohaku makes a very important distinction that comes from Japanese terminology, between Jisange, which he calls formal repentance, and Risange, which he calls formless or absolute repentance.
Formal repentance, or relative repentance, is repentance for bad deeds of body, speech and mind, however small they may be.
When we live by vow we are very concerned about even our small missteps.
Formless repentance is the endless repentance that matches the endless suffering, which is at the same time the endless Nirvana.

So when we chant the verse of repentance, *All my ancient twisted karma, from beginningless greed, hate and delusion, born through body, speech and mind, I now fully avow,* that's the Jisange, the formal repentance.
When we chant that verse we are purifying ourselves of all of our thoughtless and selfish deeds.

Formless repentance means that we enter the mind that is absolutely beyond selfishness, the mind that includes delusions and bad actions but fully forgives them and sees through them and understands them, because it sees through all separation and all duality.
That understands the mind that understands that there is no delusion.
And of course formless repentance is also the practice of zazen.
That's what we are doing when we are sitting in zazen, with our mind wide open, letting everything come and go, not trying to get rid of this or hold on to that.
Maybe if we sit here this weekend with that understanding, sometimes you sit there for a while and you feel bad.
That's one of the things that happens when you sit, because you feel bad about the things that you've done or failed to do, that you could have done to benefit other people.
Sometimes you sit with a lot of feelings of shame, all the feelings of failure that any honest human being would have to see if they looked.
Nobody would escape this scrutiny if they looked honestly.
Sometimes we sit with that, and that's good.
We let it come if it's going to come, and we let it go.
Because when we let it return to emptiness, that's formless repentance.
That's swimming in Buddha nature, and we are purified.
We actually feel that.
We'll feel that physically as we sit every day and as we conclude.
We'll feel lighter and easier with ourselves, even though while we were sitting there we might have suffered a lot.
So anyway, it's a wonderful book to have and to read, and to continue to read over and over again.
A lot of the great Japanese teachers who came here and brought the teachings are gone now.
Most of them are gone.
There's something really beautiful about the Japanese way that we will of course not continue to have in our midst.
Maybe we hope.
So Shohaku really is a treasure for that reason.
